title: Internet Creators Hit the Big Screen

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Part 08: From 2020 to today. Chapter 4: Internet Creators Hit the Big Screen.
segments.text: Part zero eight: From twenty twenty to today. Chapter four: Internet Creators Hit the Big Screen.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: From the Philippou brothers to Kane Parsons, Curry Barker and Markiplier, filmmakers who came up on YouTube traded their channels for film sets and, in 2026, dominated the horror box office.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: For nearly a century, the road to the director's chair had few doors: film school, a short screened at festivals, commercials, music videos, television. In the 2020s, another one opened, used by a generation that learned to shoot, edit and scare in front of millions of viewers on YouTube. On the opening weekend of Backrooms, at the turn of May into June 2026, the British trade magazine Screen Daily summed up the phenomenon in a headline: YouTube creators were “dominating” the U.S. box office. That season, two of the most-watched films in the United States were horror movies directed by twentysomething first-timers who had started out on their own channels. The road there, however, took nearly two decades and ran through filmmakers who used the internet first as a showcase and only later as studio, distributor and audience.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The first signs came from short films that went viral. In 2009, Uruguayan filmmaker Fede Álvarez posted ¡Ataque de Pánico! on YouTube, a roughly $300 short in which giant robots attack Montevideo. The video landed him a deal with Sam Raimi's production company and, four years later, the director's chair on Evil Dead (2013). Sweden's David F. Sandberg followed a similar path with Lights Out, a 2013 short starring his wife, Lotta Losten, that spread across Reddit: the feature version, Lights Out (2016), produced by James Wan, cost $5 million and grossed $149 million. In both cases, the internet served as a calling card. The video opened Hollywood's door, but the online audience didn't come along, and the films were marketed like any other studio horror movie.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The artist who proved that someone born on the internet could make auteur cinema about the internet itself was Bo Burnham. He started posting comic songs on YouTube in 2006, while still a teenager, became a stand-up comedian and made his directorial debut with Eighth Grade (2018), released by A24: the story of a 13-year-old girl who records advice videos that almost nobody watches. The film earned him the Directors Guild of America award for outstanding first-time feature director and the Writers Guild of America award for best original screenplay. On May 30, 2021, in the middle of the pandemic, came Inside, a Netflix special that Burnham wrote, shot, lit and edited by himself, inside a single room. The special won three Emmys, including for directing and writing, as well as a Grammy. Burnham became a touchstone for the next generation: someone who turned the language of the bedroom screen into art.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The breakthrough came from Australia. In 2013, in Adelaide, brothers Danny Philippou and Michael Philippou launched the channel RackaRacka, famous for violent parodies packed with homemade effects, such as a psychopathic Ronald McDonald and a battle between Harry Potter and the characters of Star Wars; the channel won a Streamy for best international channel. Alongside the channel, the two learned the craft on a professional set, as crew members on The Babadook (2014). The duo's first feature, Talk to Me (2023), premiered at the Adelaide Film Festival in October 2022, was bought by A24 at Sundance and hit theaters in July 2023. Made for $4.5 million, it grossed $92 million worldwide, became A24's highest-grossing horror film to date and won eight Australian Academy awards, including best film. Their second feature, Bring Her Back (2025), starring Sally Hawkins, scored 89% on Rotten Tomatoes and proved the brothers were no one-hit wonder.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Meanwhile, in Canada, Kyle Edward Ball ran the channel Bitesized Nightmares, where he re-created nightmares sent in by viewers. With about $15,000, much of it crowdfunded, he shot Skinamarink (2023) in a week, in the house where he grew up in Edmonton: just over an hour and a half of dark hallways, toys on the floor and the glow of a CRT television, about two children who wake up in the middle of the night to find that the doors and windows have vanished. After its premiere at the Fantasia Festival in July 2022, a technical glitch let the film leak, and clips spread across TikTok. In January 2023, the feature opened in U.S. theaters, where it made about $2 million. Audiences were split down the middle, but the message stuck: the aesthetic born in online horror videos worked in a dark theater.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The short that took the Backrooms from online forums to the big screen is the work of Kane Parsons, born in 2005 in Petaluma, California, the son of a visual effects artist. He was 16 when he posted on his channel Kane Pixels, on January 7, 2022, the tape of a 1990s cameraman who falls into the yellow labyrinth and is chased by a creature. The video grew into a series, and in February 2023 A24 announced the feature, with Parsons himself, then 17, directing. Backrooms (2026) opened on May 29, 2026, with Chiwetel Ejiofor and Renate Reinsve in the cast and a budget under $10 million. It debuted with $81.5 million in the United States, the biggest opening in A24's history, and made Parsons, at 20, the youngest filmmaker ever to top the North American box office. It went on to pass $400 million worldwide, with an 86% critics' score.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The season's other phenomenon came from comedy. Curry Barker, born in 1999 in Alabama, dropped out of film school in Los Angeles to make sketches for YouTube and TikTok with his friend Cooper Tomlinson as the duo that's a bad idea. In 2023, his horror short The Chair topped 10 million views and caught producers' attention; the following year, he released Milk & Serial (2024) for free on YouTube, a found footage feature that cost US$ 800. Obsession (2026), his first film made for theaters, cost at most US$ 750,000, according to Barker, and was bought by Focus Features for about US$ 15 million after the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival. Released in the U.S. on May 15, 2026, it grew in its second weekend, something extremely rare for a horror film in wide release, passed US$ 500 million worldwide and became the year's highest-grossing horror film and the biggest in Focus's history. Barker has already been tapped to direct a new version of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre for A24.

tracks.title: Learn more: Analog horror and liminal spaces: the horror born on YouTube

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Learn more: Analog horror and liminal spaces: the horror born on YouTube.
segments.text: Learn more: Analog horror and liminal spaces: the horror born on YouTube.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: On May 12, 2019, an anonymous user on 4chan's paranormal board asked for disturbing images that “felt off” and opened the thread with a photo of an empty room with carpet, yellow wallpaper and fluorescent lighting (taken in 2002 in a former furniture store in Oshkosh, Wisconsin). Another user replied with a text about an infinite maze of identical rooms: the Backrooms. The image helped popularize the aesthetic of liminal spaces, everyday places emptied of their function and strangely familiar. At the same time, analog horror was growing on YouTube, imitating VHS tapes, emergency broadcasts and 1980s and 1990s TV, with degraded images and almost no cheap jump scares. The name came from Local 58, a series by Kris Straub launched in 2015; it was followed by Gemini Home Entertainment (2019) and The Mandela Catalogue (2021). An heir to the found footage of The Blair Witch Project (1999), this kind of horror bets on what the image hides. In January 2022, a teenager brought the two currents together in a VHS-style short animated in Blender; the video went on to top 90 million views.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: If Parsons and Barker reached the movies with help from studios, Mark Fischbach, aka Markiplier, wanted to do it all himself. Since 2012, he has amassed more than 38 million subscribers playing indie horror games like Five Nights at Freddy's, whose film adaptation, Five Nights at Freddy's (2023), made US$ 297 million in 2023 with YouTubers in cameo roles and just a 33% approval rating from critics. Markiplier's own film, Iron Lung (2026), an adaptation of David Szymanski's 2022 game, was written, directed, edited, starred in and financed by Markiplier, on a budget that, according to him, came to between US$ 4 million and US$ 5 million. The plan was to show the film in 60 independent theaters. Fans began asking their local theaters to book it, and chains such as AMC, Regal and Cinemark signed on. On January 30, 2026, Iron Lung opened in more than 3,000 theaters with US$ 18.2 million, and went on to pass US$ 50 million worldwide despite mixed reviews.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The most ironic case is that of Chris Stuckmann. A YouTube film critic since 2009 with more than 2 million subscribers, he announced in 2021 that he would stop trashing bad movies (he no longer wanted to “tear down” filmmakers) and focus on discussing how films are made. His first feature, Shelby Oaks (2025), partly funded by fans on Kickstarter, follows a woman searching for her missing sister, a ghost-hunting YouTuber, and starts out as found footage before turning into a conventional narrative. After its premiere at the Fantasia Festival in 2024, it gained Mike Flanagan as executive producer and distribution from Neon, which paid for extra days of shooting. Released in October 2025, it made about US$ 8 million worldwide, earned a 55% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes and a C+ audience grade from CinemaScore. The critic who used to judge others became a target of criticism himself and discovered that loyal followers are not enough to fill theaters.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: What changes when a director arrives with an audience already in tow? For the studios, the risk seems smaller: the film is born with built-in marketing and an idea already tested in the comments. After Backrooms and Obsession, executives began scouring YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for new directors. Neon hired Sam Evenson to turn his short Mora into a feature, and Lionsgate and Blumhouse brought in Dylan Clark, a maker of YouTube horror shorts, to direct a new Blair Witch film. Skepticism, however, persists. An agent quoted by the newsletter The Ankler called the rush “embarrassing” and noted that Hollywood is “still run by 81-year-olds who don't watch YouTube.” Journalist Ryan Broderick doubted that any YouTuber, even one as big as MrBeast, could single-handedly draw crowds to a film.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In Brazil, the jump from the internet to the big screen took a different route. Back in the 2010s, the comedy group Porta dos Fundos, founded in 2012, brought its humor to theaters with Porta dos Fundos: Contrato Vitalício (2016), which sold about 460,000 tickets. That same year, It's a Fairy! (2016), starring YouTuber Kéfera Buchmann, drew 1.7 million moviegoers but was savaged by critics. In 2017, Whindersson Nunes, who then ran the country's biggest channel, shared top billing with Tom Cavalcante in Os Parças (2017), and Internet - The Movie (2017) packed several YouTubers into a single cast. In Brazil, creators came in as the stars of comedies made by the traditional industry, not as the authors of their own films. The closest thing to the American model is Luccas Neto, who, after Os Aventureiros: A Origem (2023), made with Warner, used his own company to finance Príncipe Lu e a Lenda do Dragão (2024), featuring a special appearance by comedy legend Renato Aragão.

tracks.title: Learn more: From channel to set: how to fund a film with your own audience

segments.speaker: narrador

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: For creators with an audience of their own, the public can also be the investor, the distributor and the marketing team. In 2022, Chris Stuckmann raised $1,390,845 from 14,720 backers on Kickstarter to shoot Shelby Oaks, the best-funded horror campaign in the platform's history. Markiplier went further: he paid for Iron Lung out of his own pocket, negotiated directly with theaters and said that, with no major studio in the middle, he was splitting the box office with exhibitors “basically 50/50.” He then registered with YouTube as a film distributor (a so-called aggregator), which let him release the feature on the platform itself in May 2026, with no middlemen; the DVDs and Blu-rays he printed at home. Curry Barker didn't ask fans for money, but he used his free videos as a portfolio: his feature Milk & Serial, released for free, earned him a contract with a major agency. In each case, the channel plays a different role: funding source, distributor or showcase. The model's limit is clear: an audience guarantees an opening, not word of mouth.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Film history has seen this movie before. In the 1950s, directors trained in live television, such as Sidney Lumet, arrived in Hollywood; in the 1990s, it was the turn of those who came from music videos, like David Fincher and Spike Jonze. Internet creators bring something similar: a visual language shaped in front of small screens, with handheld cameras, degraded images, empty spaces and the dread of what lies outside the frame. And they bring something new: an audience that has followed them for years, tests every idea in the comments and feels a sense of ownership over the project. The risk, as skeptics point out, is that the industry will mistake subscriber counts for talent. The bet is that, among thousands of channels, lie some of the great auteurs of the next decade.
